opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's a strange feeling. By the time a model goes public, we've lived with it for weeks or months. We've seen its best outputs, its embarrassing failures, and all the evaluation numbers. So the release itself isn't a moment of discovery for us. Internally, the excitement peaked much earlier, usually late at night when some training run finally crossed a threshold we'd been stuck on.

What release day gives me is something different: I get to see the model through other people's eyes. Users always find things we didn't anticipate. Someone uses it for a task we never benchmarked, or pushes it in a direction we never thought to test, and suddenly you learn something new about your own model. That part still surprises me every time. It's almost humbling, because you think you know it completely, and then thousands of people show you that you only knew the part you were looking at.

There's also anxiety, of course. You know the weaknesses better than anyone, so you watch the feedback partly waiting for people to hit the problems you already know are there. When they do, it's not a shock. It's more like, "Okay, yes, that's the next thing we have to fix."

So for me, a release isn't really an ending or a celebration. It's more like handing the model over to the world and getting a much bigger, more honest evaluation than anything we could run ourselves. And by then, most of the team's attention has already moved on to the next model.

r001.rationale: The response says the team knew the model’s outputs and weaknesses, but that users often surprised them with unexpected uses and findings. It does not say Fuli Luo could anticipate the public’s reaction.

r002.rationale: It describes release day as less exciting because the team had already lived with the model and excitement peaked during training. It does not attribute that muted response to anticipating the public’s reception.

r003.rationale: The release is described as a broader evaluation that teaches the team new things, including through unanticipated user behavior—not as confirmation that the public saw the capabilities the team already believed the model had.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's a strange feeling. By the time a model is released, the excitement for me happened months earlier — the moment the eval numbers came back, or the first time I chatted with a checkpoint and it did something I didn't expect. The release day itself is more like watching other people open a gift you already know what's inside.

But I'd say two things still surprise me every time.

The first is how people use it. We train on benchmarks, we test on benchmarks, but the real world is not a benchmark. Users immediately find use cases we never thought of, and they also find failures we never thought of. Within the first few days you learn more about your model's true capability boundary than in weeks of internal evaluation. So in that sense, I don't fully know the model's capabilities before release. I know its scores. That's different.

The second is the emotional side. When you've worked on something for a long time, you become a bit numb to it. You see all the flaws — this case it still gets wrong, that behavior we didn't have time to fix. Then you see someone outside post something like, "I can't believe it did this," and you remember what it felt like the first time. It kind of resets you.

So I'd say release day is less about discovering the model and more about discovering the gap between how we see it and how the world sees it. That gap is where the next version comes from.

r001.rationale: She says the release-day excitement happened earlier, but also says users’ reactions and discoveries still surprise her; she does not explain that knowing the capabilities lets her anticipate the public’s reaction.

r002.rationale: She attributes feeling numb to having worked on the model for a long time and seeing its flaws, not to anticipating its reception.

r003.rationale: She describes release as revealing a gap between the team’s view and the world’s view, not as confirmation that the public saw the capabilities the team expected.

astra-6.text: For me, the surprise comes before the release, while we’re training and testing the model. By the time it launches, I’ve already spent so much time with it that I don’t have that same feeling of discovering something new. What I’m curious about then is how other people will use it. We test the things we can think of, but users bring questions and situations we never imagined. So the release is still exciting—the excitement shifts from what the model can do to what people discover they can do with it.

r001.rationale: She says she is curious how other people will use the model and that users bring unexpected questions. She does not say her prior knowledge lets her anticipate the public’s reaction.

r002.rationale: She attributes the reduced sense of discovery to having spent so much time with the model, not to anticipating how people will receive it.

r003.rationale: The response describes excitement about what users may discover, but does not say the release confirms the public perceived capabilities her team already believed the model had.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the excitement is less about discovering what the model can do, because I’ve already spent so much time with it. It’s more about seeing how other people experience it. Internally, you develop certain habits—you know what to ask, what works, where the limitations are. Once it’s released, people bring completely different questions and use cases. So even when I know the model well, the release can still surprise me.

r001.rationale: She says public use can surprise her with different questions and use cases; she does not say prior knowledge lets her anticipate the public’s reaction.

r002.rationale: She describes less excitement about discovering capabilities, but does not attribute a muted emotional response to anticipating the model’s reception.

r003.rationale: She describes learning how others experience the model, not the release confirming that the public perceived capabilities her team already believed it had.
